title: The Odyssey
subtitle: The Long Way Home
attribution: An original abridged adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey
description: The proof of home is rooted in something no stranger could know.
intro: One last question stands between returning and being home.
ending: For this morning, no one had to leave.
stageLabel: A pixel art retelling of the Odyssey

adaptationSource.title: Homer, Odyssey, Books XXIII–XXIV
adaptationSource.note: Original abridged English narration and dialogue. Events are condensed for quiet episodic reading. Ritual sacrifice and deaths are represented without gore. The final conflict of Book XXIV is condensed to Athena intervening before renewed bloodshed.

steps.text: After the fighting, Odysseus and Telemachus waited in the hall. Eurycleia would go upstairs to tell Penelope her husband was home.
“She will think this is another dream.”
“Then let her ask what she needs to ask.”
He waited while the servants put the house in order. He had survived the sea and the hall; he could wait for her.
“Why does she not come running?”
“She has had twenty years of reasons to be careful.”
The last distance between them would not be crossed with an arrow.
After hearing Eurycleia’s news, Penelope came downstairs. She wanted proof that this man really was Odysseus.
“Mother, it is him.”
“If it is, there are things only we will know.”
Telemachus stepped away to give his parents space. Odysseus knew why Penelope was careful: strangers had lied to her before.
“You may test me.”
“I have waited so long that even hope must answer a question.”
Penelope asked Eurycleia to move their bed outside its room. It was a test: the real Odysseus would know why that was impossible.
Eurycleia led them toward the bedroom. Odysseus and Penelope left the hall to look at the bed together.

steps.text: Odysseus, Penelope and Eurycleia went from the hall to the bedroom. The bed was still where Odysseus had built it.
The bed stood in the chamber. Eurycleia reached toward its wooden frame, but it did not move.
“Who could move that bed?”
“I built it around a living olive tree. I shaped the trunk into one post and built this room around it.”
“Unless someone has cut the root, it cannot leave this place.”
Penelope recognized his answer. The rooted bed was their private secret, so she could finally be sure he was her husband.
“No one else could have told me that.”
She went to him. This time, neither disguise nor doubt stood between them.
They held each other beside the bed that had stayed rooted through every year he was gone.
“I was afraid of being deceived.”
“You kept something safe that I could not see.”
They spoke of the journeys he had survived, and the days she had kept from closing on her. There was so much to tell.
Not every loss could be repaired by returning. His mother was gone. His companions would not follow him through the door.
His mother had died, but his father, Laertes, was still alive. The next morning, Odysseus and Telemachus would walk to his orchard.
One more person had spent the years waiting. One more recognition remained.
When morning came, Odysseus left Penelope in their room. Telemachus would meet him outside and walk with him to Laertes.

steps.text: Odysseus and Telemachus followed the path from the palace to Laertes’s orchard. The old man was working among his trees.
Laertes looked up in the orchard clearing. Odysseus named the fruit trees his father had given him as a boy.
“You remember them.”
“You taught me their names.”
The dead suitors’ families had heard about the fighting. Angry and grieving, they came looking for Odysseus.
Laertes came closer to his son. Then a man arrived to speak for the suitors’ families. He wanted them to fight again.
Athena stepped between the men and ordered them to stop. Odysseus listened. Another fight would only bring more loss.
“Enough. Let this land live.”
There would be work after the journey: a house to mend, a kingdom to steady, years to learn about one another.
With peace agreed, Odysseus could stay with his family at last. There was work ahead, but his long journey home was over.
